claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in nanoscale FCC/BCC HEA multilayers under sustained intermediate-temperature loading is governed primarily by partial-dislocation nucleation and glide.
Local short-range order at FCC/BCC interfaces moderates the proposed partial-dislocation mechanism.
Interfacial short-range order promotes intermittent dislocation activity and stable accumulation of plastic strain over time.
The proposed initial multilayers have uniform nanoscale layer thicknesses, intentionally prepared SRO, minimal preexisting defects, controlled compositions, and stable interfaces.
Applied stress and temperature will be varied during in-situ nanoindentation creep testing while simulations track partial-dislocation activity and interfacial SRO.
SRO at or near FCC/BCC interfaces and within HEA layers modifies dislocation structure and mobility.
Partial dislocations repeatedly nucleate at or near the FCC/BCC interfaces.
Severe lattice distortion promotes dislocation nucleation while impeding long-range dislocation glide.
SRO regions at FCC/BCC interfaces concentrate lattice strain energy.
SRO-induced concentration of lattice strain energy hinders long-range glide and produces creep dominated by intermittent partial-dislocation motion.
Relative to reduced-SRO or compositionally simpler baselines, SRO-containing multilayers will have lower but persistent creep rates.
Regions with greater local SRO will contain stable pinned partial dislocations.
SRO-containing multilayers will show a more pronounced time-dependent accumulation of lattice defects under constant load.
Reduced-SRO or compositionally simpler baseline multilayers will exhibit more conventional dislocation glide and transition more rapidly to steady-state creep.
The proposed mechanism dominates only when SRO is sufficiently developed to impede glide and layer thickness is between 10 and 100 nm.
Extreme temperatures or stresses well beyond yield may shift deformation to a different controlling mechanism.
Grain-boundary or interface diffusional creep may compete with partial-dislocation activity depending on composition, temperature, and stress.
Failure to observe either significantly reduced but sustained creep rates in SRO-enhanced samples or interfacial partial-dislocation activity would falsify the proposed dominant mechanism.
